source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper II
question:
In Frances Burney's Evelina, the heroine comes out in society in two places. Which two?
(a) Bath
(b) Bristol
(c) Leeds
(d) London
infoBite: Evelina (1778), published anonymously, is subtitled 'The History of a Young Lady's Entrance into the World'. It is epistolary; the action moves between London and Bristol Hotwells.

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper II
question: Which Shakespeare line is repeated several times in Virginia Woolf's Mrs Dalloway?

options.A: "If music be the food of love, play on"
options.B: "Fear no more the heat of the sun, / Nor the furious winter's rages"
options.C: "Those are pearls that were his eyes"
options.D: "There is a tide in the affairs of men"

infoBite: The dirge 'Fear no more the heat o' the sun' is from Cymbeline (Act 4, Scene 2). It runs through the minds of both Clarissa and Septimus Smith.

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper II
question:
Identify the important theatres of the Elizabethan period:
(a) Peacock
(b) Globe
(c) Swan
(d) Grand
infoBite: The Theatre (1576), the Curtain, the Rose (1587), the Swan (1595) and the Globe (1599) were the main Elizabethan playhouses. The famous drawing of an Elizabethan stage is of the Swan.

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper II
question: In which poem does Matthew Arnold describe himself as 'Wandering between two worlds, one dead, / The other powerless to be born'?
infoBite: 'Stanzas from the Grande Chartreuse' (1855) is set in the Carthusian monastery near Grenoble; it voices Victorian loss of faith, like 'Dover Beach' (1867).

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper II
question: Who said, "All modern American literature comes from one book by Mark Twain called Huckleberry Finn"?
infoBite: Hemingway wrote it in Green Hills of Africa (1935). Huckleberry Finn (1884) is narrated in Huck's vernacular voice.

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper II
question: Who popularised the emblem-book genre in English with Emblems (1635)?
infoBite: Quarles's Emblems (1635) pairs devotional verses with engraved pictures; it was the most popular verse book of the century. Herbert's 'Easter Wings' shows a similar visual habit.

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper II
question: Which work of Byron begins with the lines "I want a hero: an uncommon want, / When every year and month sends forth a new one"?
infoBite: Don Juan (1819–24) is in ottava rima (abababcc). The same opening line was asked again in NET January 2017 Paper II.

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper II
question: The title of Sir Thomas Browne's Religio Medici means:
infoBite: Religio Medici (1643) is a physician's statement of faith. Browne also wrote Urn Burial (Hydriotaphia) and The Garden of Cyrus (1658).

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper II
question: Which recent novel is a retelling of Sophocles's Antigone?
infoBite: Home Fire (2017) recasts Antigone among British Pakistani siblings (Isma, Aneeka, Parvaiz). It won the Women's Prize for Fiction in 2018.

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper II
question:
Identify the two important works of Paul de Man:
(a) Blindness and Insight
(b) Allegories of Reading
(c) Theoretical Essays
(d) Criticism and Ideology
infoBite: De Man's Blindness and Insight (1971) and Allegories of Reading (1979) are key Yale School texts. Criticism and Ideology (1976) is Terry Eagleton's.

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper II
question: Samuel Johnson wrote, "About the beginning of the seventeenth century appeared a race of writers that may be termed the metaphysical poets." In which of his Lives of the Poets does this appear?
infoBite: In the 'Life of Cowley' (1779) Johnson defines metaphysical wit as 'heterogeneous ideas … yoked by violence together' (discordia concors).

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper II
question: "The terms of the contract are not disagreeable to me." This is an example of:
infoBite: Litotes is understatement that affirms by denying the opposite ('not bad', 'no mean city'). Its opposite is hyperbole.

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper II
question: Who wrote the lines "To see a World in a Grain of Sand / And a Heaven in a Wild Flower"?
infoBite: These open Blake's 'Auguries of Innocence' (written c. 1803, published 1863), followed by 'Hold Infinity in the palm of your hand'.

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper II
question: In D. H. Lawrence's Women in Love, what is Winifred's Pekinese dog called?
infoBite: Winifred Crich is Gerald's young sister. Women in Love (1920) is the sequel to The Rainbow (1915), following Ursula and Gudrun Brangwen.

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper II
question: Which New Critic put forward the idea of 'the heresy of paraphrase'?
infoBite: 'The Heresy of Paraphrase' is the last chapter of Brooks's The Well Wrought Urn (1947): a poem's meaning cannot be reduced to a prose statement.

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper II
question: Edmund Spenser's Colin Clouts Come Home Againe is a fine example of:
infoBite: Colin Clout is Spenser's pastoral persona, first used in The Shepheardes Calender (1579). The 1595 poem describes his visit to Elizabeth's court.

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper II
question: In An Essay of Dramatic Poesy, whom does Dryden call "the most learned and judicious Writer which any Theater ever had"?
infoBite: Dryden (1668) admires Jonson but loves Shakespeare: 'I admire him, but I love Shakespeare.' Shakespeare had 'the largest and most comprehensive soul'.

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper II
question: This Australian poet grew up in rural New South Wales, published her first book of poems in 1946 and co-founded the Wildlife Preservation Society of Queensland in 1962. Identify her.
infoBite: Judith Wright's first collection was The Moving Image (1946). Her poem 'Bora Ring' (asked in Paper III of the same exam) mourns lost Aboriginal culture.

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper II
question: Aphra Behn's Oroonoko is set in:
infoBite: Oroonoko (1688) follows an enslaved African prince in the English colony of Surinam. Behn was among the first Englishwomen to earn a living by writing.

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper II
question: Who published the first collected edition of Gerard Manley Hopkins's poems in 1918?
infoBite: Hopkins died in 1889; his friend Robert Bridges, then Poet Laureate, brought out the Poems in 1918. Hopkins coined 'sprung rhythm', 'inscape' and 'instress'.

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper II
question: Samuel Richardson named his heroine Pamela after a character in:
infoBite: Pamela is a princess in Sidney's Arcadia (published 1590), where the name was coined. Richardson's Pamela (1740) is subtitled 'Virtue Rewarded'.

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper II
question: Pinter once said he first grasped the dramatic power of the pause from a popular American comedian. Who?
infoBite: Jack Benny was famous for his long, deadpan pauses. Pinter's pauses and silences are central to The Birthday Party (1958) and The Homecoming (1965).
note: The literariness.org key gave a different answer; the CBSE final key is followed here. (literariness gave Charlie Chaplin.)

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper II
question: Charles Dickens's Bleak House is pointedly critical of England's:
infoBite: Bleak House (1852–53) centres on the endless Chancery suit Jarndyce and Jarndyce. It opens in London fog.

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper II
question: Which of the following is NOT true of the ideal state in Thomas More's Utopia?

options.A: Personal property, money and vice are effectively abolished.
options.B: The root causes of crime, ambition and political conflict are eliminated.
options.C: There is only one religion, guided by the principle of a benevolent Supreme Being.
options.D: Its priesthood, which includes some women, is limited in number.

infoBite: Utopia (1516, in Latin) allows many religions and practises toleration; most Utopians worship one supreme power, but no single religion is imposed.
note: The literariness.org key gave a different answer; the CBSE final key is followed here. (literariness gave option 4.)

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper II
question: Which character created by Coleridge gives the account "Five warriors seized me yestermorn, / Me, even me, a maid forlorn"?

options.D: The maid who appeared in Christabel's dream

infoBite: In Christabel (Part I, 1816) the mysterious Geraldine tells this story to win Christabel's pity; the poem was left unfinished.

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper II
question: Which Thomas Hardy novel opens with a gloomy description of Egdon Heath?
infoBite: The Return of the Native (1878) opens with 'A Face on which Time makes but little Impression' — Egdon Heath. Eustacia Vye and Clym Yeobright are its central pair.

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper II
question: What is the metrical form of John Gower's Confessio Amantis?
infoBite: Confessio Amantis (c. 1390) is a lover's confession to Genius, priest of Venus, in some 33,000 octosyllabic lines. Chaucer called him 'moral Gower'.

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper II
question: What happens to the lock of hair at the end of Pope's The Rape of the Lock?

options.A: It is given back to its rightful owner.
options.B: It is preserved in a monument.
options.D: It is presented to the poet as a token of gratitude.

infoBite: In Canto V the lock rises to the heavens as a new star — a parody of Berenice's lock in Callimachus and Catullus.
note: The literariness.org key gave a different answer; the CBSE final key is followed here. (literariness gave option 4.)

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper II
question: "The Bard. The Iron Lady. The King." These are examples of:
infoBite: Antonomasia replaces a proper name with an epithet ('the Bard' for Shakespeare) or uses a proper name for a type ('a Solomon'). Aposiopesis breaks off mid-sentence.

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper II
question: Which Margaret Atwood novel depicts the notorious murders committed in 1843?
infoBite: Alias Grace (1996) is based on Grace Marks, convicted in the 1843 murders of Thomas Kinnear and Nancy Montgomery in Upper Canada.

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper II
question: Which W. B. Yeats poem rejects the sensual world in favour of "the artifice of eternity"?
infoBite: 'Sailing to Byzantium' opens The Tower (1928): 'That is no country for old men.' Its lines were also asked in GATE 2025.

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper II
question: Which character in Moby-Dick falls overboard and goes insane as a result?
infoBite: Pip, the Black cabin boy, is abandoned in the sea and loses his mind; Ahab takes him into his cabin. Moby-Dick (1851) opens 'Call me Ishmael'.

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper II
question: Which Seamus Heaney poem is dedicated to the Irish poet Paul Muldoon?
infoBite: 'Widgeon (for Paul Muldoon)' is in Station Island (1984). Heaney won the Nobel Prize in 1995.
note: The literariness.org key gave a different answer; the CBSE final key is followed here. (literariness gave 'A Migration'.)

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper II
question: In William Golding's Lord of the Flies, which character is put to death?
infoBite: Simon is killed by the boys in a frenzied dance; Piggy is killed by the boulder Roger releases. Ralph escapes and Jack leads the hunters.
note: The CBSE final key accepts both (1) Piggy and (3) Simon. In the app, tap both.

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper II
question: In The Canterbury Tales, who has a fire-red face full of sores?
infoBite: The Summoner has a 'fyr-reed cherubynnes face' with pimples. He and the Pardoner end the General Prologue's gallery of corrupt churchmen.

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper II
question: What is the term for the pace of speech?
infoBite: Tempo is the speed of speech; pitch, loudness and tempo together form prosody. Pitch patterns across a sentence make intonation.

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper II
question:
Match the titles with the authors:
(a) Sexual Politics
(b) A Literature of Their Own
(c) Thinking About Women
(d) The Laugh of the Medusa

(i) Mary Ellmann
(ii) Elaine Showalter
(iii) Hélène Cixous
(iv) Kate Millett
infoBite: Ellmann 1968, Millett 1970, Cixous 1975 (écriture féminine), Showalter 1977 (gynocriticism; Feminine–Feminist–Female phases).

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper II
question: Which historical event does Tennyson's "The Charge of the Light Brigade" describe?
works: The Charge of the Light Brigade
infoBite: The charge took place at Balaclava on 25 October 1854; Tennyson wrote the poem weeks later as Poet Laureate. 'Theirs not to reason why'.

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper II
question: Which of the following is NOT one of the four essays of Northrop Frye's Anatomy of Criticism?
infoBite: The fourth essay is 'Rhetorical Criticism: Theory of Genres'. Anatomy of Criticism (1957) maps the four mythoi: comedy, romance, tragedy, irony/satire.

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper II
question: In Robert Browning's "Andrea del Sarto", which painter does Andrea NOT compare himself with?
infoBite: Andrea, 'the faultless painter', measures himself against Raphael, Michelangelo and Leonardo: 'Ah, but a man's reach should exceed his grasp'. In Men and Women (1855).

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper II
question: In Swift's Gulliver's Travels, what does Gulliver call William Dampier, the writer of voyages?
infoBite: In the prefatory letter Gulliver mentions 'my cousin Dampier'. Dampier's A New Voyage Round the World (1697) was a model for Swift's mock-travel book (1726).

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper II
question: Which of the following is NOT a character in Pride and Prejudice?
infoBite: Miss Bates is the talkative spinster of Emma (1815), whom Emma insults at Box Hill.

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper II
question: Which character in Shakespeare's As You Like It speaks the "All the world's a stage" lines?
infoBite: Melancholy Jaques gives the 'seven ages of man' speech in Act 2, Scene 7; Touchstone is the court fool.

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper II
question: Which rivers are named in Andrew Marvell's "To His Coy Mistress"?
infoBite: 'Thou by the Indian Ganges' side / Shouldst rubies find: I by the tide / Of Humber would complain.' The poem is a carpe diem argument in three parts.

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper II
question: "The truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth" is an example of:
infoBite: Ploce repeats a word with other words in between; epizeuxis repeats it with nothing in between ('Words, words, words').
note: The literariness.org key gave a different answer; the CBSE final key is followed here. (literariness gave epizeuxis.)

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper II
question: Which of these is NOT an image in W. H. Auden's "In Memory of W. B. Yeats"?

options.A: Mercury sinking in the mouth of the dying day
options.B: Wolves running through the evergreen forests

works: In Memory of W. B. Yeats
infoBite: The elegy (1939) opens 'He disappeared in the dead of winter'; Part II says 'poetry makes nothing happen' (asked in GATE 2023).

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper II
question: Who wrote Steps to the Temple?
infoBite: Crashaw's Steps to the Temple (1646) honours Herbert's The Temple (1633). Crashaw became a Catholic; his 'The Flaming Heart' is on St Teresa.

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper II
question:
Match the characters with the works:
(a) Jim Dixon
(b) Jimmy Porter
(c) Joe Lampton
(d) Charles Lumley

(i) Room at the Top
(ii) Hurry on Down
(iii) Look Back in Anger
(iv) Lucky Jim
infoBite: Angry Young Men: Wain's Hurry on Down (1953), Amis's Lucky Jim (1954), Osborne's Look Back in Anger (1956), Braine's Room at the Top (1957).
note: The literariness.org key gave a different answer; the CBSE final key is followed here. (literariness gave option 4.)

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper II
question:
In Book I of The Prelude, Wordsworth says he grew up "fostered alike by ___ and by ___". Pick the right pair:
(a) nature
(b) fear
(c) imagination
(d) beauty
infoBite: 'Fair seed-time had my soul, and I grew up / Fostered alike by beauty and by fear' (1850 text, Book I). The stolen-boat and bird-snaring episodes follow.
note: The literariness.org key gave a different answer; the CBSE final key is followed here. (literariness gave option 4.)

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper II
question: The title of Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o's Petals of Blood comes from a poem by Derek Walcott. Which poem?
infoBite: Petals of Blood (1977) is set in post-independence Kenya (Ilmorog). Its epigraph is from Walcott's 'The Swamp'.

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper III
question: Which Byron poem tells of a Venetian wife who, believing her husband lost at sea, takes a lover — until he returns?
infoBite: Beppo (1818) was Byron's first poem in ottava rima, the comic stanza he then used in Don Juan.

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper III
question: Who wrote the poem "Our Casuarina Tree"?
works: Ancient Ballads and Legends of Hindustan
infoBite: Toru Dutt (1856–77) wrote in English and French; the poem appeared in Ancient Ballads and Legends of Hindustan (1882). It was a GATE 2026 option too.

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper III
question: Identify the Jacobean political satire in which the Black King (Spain and the Jesuits) is checkmated by the White Knight (Prince Charles), and which James I suppressed.

options.D: The Knight of the Burning Pestle

infoBite: Middleton's A Game at Chess (1624) ran nine days at the Globe before it was banned. A King and No King is Beaumont and Fletcher's; The Wonderful Yeare is Dekker's pamphlet.

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper III
question: Fredric Jameson associated postmodern culture with ______ capitalism.
works: Postmodernism, or, The Cultural Logic of Late Capitalism
infoBite: Jameson borrowed Ernest Mandel's three stages: market, monopoly (imperialist) and late, multinational capitalism. Pastiche and 'depthlessness' are his postmodern features.

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper III
question: In Evelyn Waugh's A Handful of Dust, what is the name of the mule in the story John Andrew tells his father?
infoBite: A Handful of Dust (1934) takes its title from Eliot's The Waste Land. Tony Last ends up reading Dickens aloud forever in the Amazon jungle.

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper III
question: In which year was the Oxford English Dictionary published in twelve volumes under its present title?
infoBite: The dictionary, edited first by James Murray, came out in parts from 1884 as A New English Dictionary on Historical Principles. The 1933 reissue took the title OED.

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper III
question: In which volume of The Life and Opinions of Tristram Shandy, Gentleman does Tristram finally narrate his birth?
infoBite: Tristram is born in Volume III (1761), where the Author's Preface also appears late. The novel runs to nine volumes (1759–67).

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper III
question:
Cervantes's Don Quixote foreshadows metafiction when the novelist:
(a) says the first chapters are recreated from the Archive of La Mancha
(b) says it is a faithful rendering of a Catalan text in Spanish
(c) says part of it has been translated from the Arabic of the Moorish author Cide Hamete Benengeli
(d) says he is rewriting the history of a medieval knight, mixing the heroic with the farcical
The right combination is:
infoBite: The narrator claims to have found the rest of the story in Arabic manuscripts by Cide Hamete Benengeli, bought in Toledo. Don Quixote appeared in 1605 and 1615.
note: The literariness.org key gave a different answer; the CBSE final key is followed here. (literariness gave option 4.)

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper III
question: In Plato's theory of mimesis, which common object does he use to show that art is an imitation of an imitation?
infoBite: In Republic Book X: God makes the Form of the bed/couch, the carpenter a copy, the painter a copy of the copy — art is 'thrice removed' from truth.

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper III
question: Who translated the Bhagvat-Geeta (1784), which William Jones admired?
infoBite: Wilkins's Bhagvat-Geeta, published in London in 1785 with a preface by Warren Hastings dated 1784, was the first direct English translation of a Sanskrit text.

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper III
question: Which play has the characters Coll, Gib, Daw and Mak?
infoBite: It belongs to the Wakefield (Towneley) cycle; Mak the sheep-stealer hides a lamb in a cradle, a comic parody of the Nativity.

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper III
question:
In Milan Kundera's The Unbearable Lightness of Being, which are Tereza's recurring nightmares?
(a) cats attacking her
(b) wolves attacking her
(c) being dead and buried in a common grave among strangers
(d) being dead, stripped, and surrounded by other naked corpses
infoBite: Tereza's dreams of cats and of marching naked with other women express her jealousy over Tomas. The novel (1984) is set around the 1968 Prague Spring.
note: The literariness.org key gave a different answer; the CBSE final key is followed here. (literariness gave option 1.)

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper III
question: Which Coleridge poem closely echoes the opening of Wordsworth's Immortality Ode?
infoBite: 'The Mad Monk' (1800) has 'There was a time when earth, and sea, and skies…', echoing Wordsworth's 'There was a time when meadow, grove, and stream'.

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper III
question: Which statement about the enchanted world of Christina Rossetti's "Goblin Market" is NOT true?

options.A: Laura gives a lock of her hair and a tear in exchange for the goblin fruit.
options.B: Jeanie, who ate the fruit, dwindled and sought the goblins day and night.
options.C: Laura goes to the market again, sees no goblins and hears only their shrill cries.
options.D: Laura's hair thins and greys, and she fades towards decay like a waning moon.

infoBite: Goblin Market (1862): Laura pays with a golden curl; Lizzie later saves her. After tasting, Laura can no longer even hear the goblins' cry.

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper III
question: In which prison was Defoe's Moll Flanders born?
infoBite: Moll Flanders (1722) is born in Newgate and returns there as a thief before transportation to Virginia.

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper III
question: In which poem does Judith Wright lament the erasure of Aboriginal culture?
infoBite: 'Bora Ring' (The Moving Image, 1946) mourns an abandoned Aboriginal ceremonial ground. Wright appears in Paper II of the same exam too.

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper III
question: Early in Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four, Winston Smith gets hard evidence of the Party's dishonesty. What is it?

options.A: Emmanuel Goldstein's confession that he is a Party operative, not an enemy
options.B: O'Brien's diary entry hinting that Big Brother does not exist
options.C: A photograph proving that three accused men were out of the country when their crime took place
options.D: A colleague's revelation that Inner Party members destroyed historical records and created false ones

infoBite: The photograph shows Jones, Aaronson and Rutherford in New York on the day they confessed to being in Eurasia. Winston drops it down the memory hole.

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper III
question: The Indian Queen is:

options.A: a heroic tragedy in rhymed couplets by John Dryden
options.B: a long free-verse poem by Keki Daruwalla
options.C: an autobiography of an Indian princess in exile
options.D: a fictional life of Maharani Gayatri Devi

infoBite: The Indian Queen (1664), written with Sir Robert Howard, is set in Mexico; Purcell later set it as a semi-opera. Its sequel is The Indian Emperour (1665).

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper III
question: In J. M. Coetzee's Disgrace, David Lurie works on an opera about which Romantic poet?
infoBite: Lurie's opera is 'Byron in Italy', about Byron and Teresa Guiccioli. Disgrace (1999) won Coetzee his second Booker.

source: UGC NET November 2017 (5 Nov 2017, CBSE) · Paper III
question:
Assertion (A): The myth has no unity or absolute source.
Reason (R): The focus or source of the myth is always a shadowy, never-actualised virtuality, so to look for a unity of discourse in myth is misplaced.

options.A: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
options.B: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

infoBite: This is Lévi-Strauss's claim in The Raw and the Cooked, quoted by Derrida in 'Structure, Sign and Play' (1966) to show a structure with no centre.

question:
Read Thomas Hardy's poem "The Voice" and answer:

Woman much missed, how you call to me, call to me,
Saying that now you are not as you were
When you had changed from the one who was all to me,
But as at first, when our day was fair.

Can it be you that I hear? Let me view you, then,
Standing as when I drew near to the town
Where you would wait for me: yes, as I knew you then,
Even to the original air-blue gown!

Or is it only the breeze, in its listlessness
Travelling across the wet mead to me here,
You being ever dissolved to wan wistlessness,
Heard no more again far or near?

Thus I; faltering forward,
Leaves around me falling,
Wind oozing thin through the thorn from norward,
And the woman calling.

What in the opening stanza suggests a woman won or a woman lost?
infoBite: "The Voice" (December 1912) belongs to Poems of 1912–13, Hardy's elegies for his first wife Emma Gifford, who died in November 1912 after years of estrangement.

source: UGC NET December 2014 (28 Dec 2014, CBSE) · Paper III
question:
Read Emily Dickinson's poem and answer:

A Bird came down the Walk —
He did not know I saw —
He bit an Angleworm in halves
And ate the fellow, raw,

And then he drank a Dew
From a convenient Grass —
And then hopped sidewise to the Wall
To let a Beetle pass —

He glanced with rapid eyes
That hurried all around —
They looked like frightened Beads, I thought —
He stirred his Velvet Head

Like one in danger, Cautious,
I offered him a Crumb
And he unrolled his feathers
And rowed him softer home —

Than Oars divide the Ocean,
Too silver for a seam —
Or Butterflies, off Banks of Noon
Leap, plashless as they swim.

Is "a convenient Grass" an example of transferred epithet?

options.A: Yes. The "convenience" of the grass is transferred from the bird to the poet, who finds the grass convenient of access.
options.B: Yes. The grass is not "convenient"; the quality is transferred from the bird, who finds the grass convenient of access.
options.C: No. It is a regular epithet.
options.D: No. It is not an epithet in the strict sense.

works: A Bird came down the Walk
infoBite: A transferred epithet (hypallage) moves an adjective from the person or thing it fits to another, as in "a sleepless night". The poem was first published in 1891.
note: Answer from the ugenglish.in solved paper (its key carries CBSE's "marks to all" rulings), checked by Claude. No official CBSE key for this paper could be found.

A "mythical norm" is endemic to societies
1. where racial myths are prevalent and widely respected, and "we" and "they" groups are created through everyday speech.

question:

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper II
question: "The pen is mightier than the sword" is an example of:
infoBite: Metonymy names a thing by something closely associated with it: the pen stands for writing, the sword for military force. The line is from Bulwer-Lytton's play Richelieu (1839).

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper II
question: An epilogue is:

options.A: prefixed to a text it introduces
options.B: suffixed to a text it sums up or extends
options.C: a piece that formally begins a book
options.D: a piece bearing no relation to the text at hand

infoBite: An epilogue is a concluding section (e.g. Prospero's speech at the end of The Tempest); a prologue is its opposite at the start.

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question:
The animal imagery in Ben Jonson's Volpone includes:
(a) the fox and the vulture
(b) the fly and the cockroach
(c) the fly, the crow and the raven
(d) the fox, the vulture and the goat
infoBite: Volpone = fox, Mosca = fly, Voltore = vulture, Corbaccio = raven, Corvino = crow. The play is a beast fable on greed (1606).

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question: Salman Rushdie's "Imaginary Homelands" is:

options.B: an essay proposing an anti-essentialist view of place
options.C: an existential lament on triumphant colonialism
options.D: an orientalist description of his favourite homelands

infoBite: The title essay (1982) of Imaginary Homelands (1991) argues that the migrant writer's India is necessarily 'imaginary', remade from broken fragments of memory.

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question:
Identify the incorrect statements about BASIC English:
(a) It was begun by C. K. Ogden and I. A. Richards around 1926 and lasted until about 1940.

(c) BASIC English aimed to reduce the essential vocabulary to 850 words.

infoBite: BASIC = British American Scientific International Commercial English, set out in Ogden's Basic English (1930) with 850 words.

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question: In what order do the following items appear in a published book?
infoBite: Front matter (title, copyright page, contents) → body with footnotes → back matter (bibliography, then index last).

question:

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question: Identify the statement about stage directions in drama that is NOT TRUE:

options.A: They tell readers how to stage, perform or imagine the play.

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question:
The emergence of the concept of "world literature" is associated with:
(a) Friedrich Schiller
(b) Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
(c) Johann Gottfried Herder
(d) Immanuel Kant
infoBite: Goethe popularised 'Weltliteratur' in conversations with Eckermann (1827); Herder's ideas of folk and national literatures laid the ground.

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question: Günter Grass's The Tin Drum is part of the Danzig Trilogy. The other two parts are:

options.B: The Rat and Cat and Mouse
options.C: Cat and Mouse and Dog Years

infoBite: Danzig Trilogy: The Tin Drum (1959), Cat and Mouse (1961), Dog Years (1963). Grass won the Nobel Prize in 1999.

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question: In a Jane Austen novel, a hostess proudly declares that her family can afford to keep a cook and her daughters have nothing to do in the kitchen. Who is this proud mother?
infoBite: Mrs. Bennet says this to Mr. Collins in Pride and Prejudice (1813), when he asks which of her fair cousins cooked the dinner.

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question: In Keats's lines "O for a beaker full of the warm South, / Full of the true, the blushful Hippocrene", what is Hippocrene?

options.B: A spring sacred to the Muses
options.C: Mount Helicon, produced from a blow of Pegasus

infoBite: Hippocrene ('horse's fountain') sprang on Mount Helicon where Pegasus struck the ground with his hoof; it was sacred to the Muses. From 'Ode to a Nightingale' (1819), stanza 2.

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question:
Which of the following statements about Wordsworth's The Prelude is not true?
(a) It was published posthumously.
(b) It records the poet's development as a poet.
(c) It runs to 14 books, and at crucial stages the poet celebrates sublime natural scenery in developing his spiritual, moral and imaginative nature.
(d) "Michael", "The Old Cumberland Beggar", "She dwelt among the untrodden ways" and "Nutting" are highlights of this volume.
infoBite: The Prelude (1850, 14 books; a 13-book version dates from 1805) appeared after Wordsworth's death. The four poems in (d) are from the 1800 Lyrical Ballads.

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question:
Assertion (A): At the end of Heart of Darkness, Marlow lies to the Intended about Kurtz's last words, telling her that he said her name.
Reason (R): Marlow lies because he is secretly in love with the Intended and tells her what she wants to hear.

options.A: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
options.B: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

infoBite: Kurtz's real last words are 'The horror! The horror!'; Marlow, who hates a lie, tells the Intended 'The last word he pronounced was — your name.'
note: Answer from UGC's updated answer key for June 2012 (after grievances). CBSE's key gives B. Many readers would say R is false (Marlow lies to protect her illusion, not out of love), which points to C — worth knowing if this pattern comes up.

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question:
Ear-training in ELT is most easily achieved through:
(a) composition
(b) dictation
(c) cloze tests
(d) listening exercises
(e) précis writing
infoBite: Dictation and listening exercises train the ear; composition, cloze tests and précis writing mainly test writing and reading.

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question: Shakespeare's Julius Caesar, Antony and Cleopatra and Coriolanus are based on:
infoBite: Shakespeare used Sir Thomas North's translation (1579) of Plutarch's Lives for his Roman plays; Holinshed's Chronicles supplied the English history plays, Macbeth and Lear.

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question: The Renaissance worldview that saw creation as ordered in a hierarchy from God down to the lowest creature, with man between the animals and the angels, is known as:
infoBite: Studied in Lovejoy's The Great Chain of Being (1936) and Tillyard's The Elizabethan World Picture (1943); Ulysses's 'degree' speech in Troilus and Cressida is a famous expression of it.

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question: In Virginia Woolf's To the Lighthouse, the lighthouse does NOT symbolise:

options.A: permanence at the heart of change
options.C: celebration of life in the heart of death
options.D: celebration of order in the heart of chaos

infoBite: To the Lighthouse (1927) has three parts — 'The Window', 'Time Passes', 'The Lighthouse'; the lighthouse stands for stability amid flux, and Lily Briscoe completes her painting at the end.

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question:
Identify the author of the following critical passage:
"Can one imagine any private soldier, in the nineties or now, reading Barrack-Room Ballads and feeling that here was a writer who spoke for him? It is very hard to do so…" The critic goes on to say that when this author writes about 'loyal' Indians the 'Salaam, sahib' motif is carried to sometimes disgusting lengths, yet he shows far more interest in the common soldier, and more concern that he get a fair deal, than most liberals of his day — he sees that the soldier is neglected, meanly underpaid and hypocritically despised by the people whose incomes he safeguards.

options.B: Malcolm Muggeridge on E. M. Forster's India
options.C: T. S. Eliot on Rudyard Kipling

infoBite: From Orwell's essay 'Rudyard Kipling' (1942), a review of Eliot's A Choice of Kipling's Verse; Orwell calls Kipling 'a jingo imperialist' but also 'a good bad poet'.

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question: In Marvell's "To His Coy Mistress", the word "coy" means:
infoBite: 'Coy' here means shy or reserved (playing hard to get). The poem is a carpe diem argument: 'Had we but world enough, and time'.

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question: From the following list, identify the back-formations: sulk, bulk, stoke, poke, swindle, bundle.
infoBite: A back-formation removes a supposed affix from an existing word: sulk (from sulky), stoke (from stoker), swindle (from swindler). Bulk, poke and bundle are not back-formations.
note: Answer from UGC's updated answer key for June 2012 (after grievances). CBSE's key gives D, even though D is the group with no back-formations. Sulk, stoke and swindle are the back-formations, and no option lists exactly those three.

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question: Read the description of a critical approach: it blurs the boundaries between literary, non-literary and cultural texts and shows how they circulate through and shape one another (its exponents speak of the 'textuality of history' and the 'historicity of texts'). What does "it" refer to?
infoBite: Stephen Greenblatt coined 'New Historicism' (1982); Louis Montrose's phrase is 'the historicity of texts and the textuality of history'.

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question: Fill in the blank: "For, though I've no idea / What this accoutred, frowsty ______ is worth, / It pleases me to stand in silence here."
infoBite: From Larkin's 'Church Going' (The Less Deceived, 1955); the speaker calls the church 'A serious house on serious earth'.

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question: Which of the following is NOT a Partition novel?
infoBite: That Long Silence (1988, Sahitya Akademi Award) is Shashi Deshpande's novel about Jaya, a silenced middle-class wife. Azadi is by Chaman Nahal and Tamas by Bhisham Sahni.

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question: Which of the following characters does not appear in V. S. Naipaul's A House for Mr Biswas?
infoBite: Ralph Singh is the narrator of Naipaul's The Mimic Men (1967). In A House for Mr Biswas (1961), Raghu is Mohun's father, Dehuti his sister and Tara his aunt.

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question: Who first used the vampire in English literature?
infoBite: John Stagg's poem 'The Vampyre' (1810) came before Polidori's prose tale The Vampyre (1819), written at Byron's Villa Diodati, and Stoker's Dracula (1897).

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question: "Universal grammar" is so called because it is:

options.A: a set of basic grammatical principles that people universally follow and easily recognise
options.B: a set of basic grammatical principles assumed to be fundamental to all natural languages
options.C: a set of advanced grammatical principles assumed to be fundamental to all natural languages
options.D: a set of universally respected practices that have come to be known as grammar

infoBite: Chomsky's Universal Grammar is the innate set of principles (with parameters) common to all human languages, which underlies the language acquisition device.

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question: Tolstoy's Anna Karenina opens: "Happy families are all alike; every unhappy family is unhappy in its own way." In the Oblonsky household, the husband's affair was with:

question: Which periodical declared that it aimed to enliven morality with wit and temper wit with morality, to bring philosophy out of closets and libraries, schools and colleges, to dwell in clubs and assemblies, at tea-tables and in coffee-houses, and that it promoted family, marriage and courtesy?

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question:

options.A: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
options.B: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

infoBite: 'Tam o' Shanter' (1791) is a narrative poem by Robert Burns, not John Clare. Clare, the 'Northamptonshire peasant poet', wrote Poems Descriptive of Rural Life and Scenery and 'I Am'.

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question:

note: CBSE did not evaluate this question (marked X in its updated key). Answer checked by Claude: it is in verse and appeared in 1711, so (c) and (d) are the incorrect statements.

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question: "Register" is:

options.D: a variety of language that professionals use in informal, non-professional settings

infoBite: Halliday describes register in terms of field (subject), tenor (relationship) and mode (spoken or written) — for example legal, medical or scientific registers.

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question: Jeremy Collier's A Short View of the Immorality and Profaneness of the English Stage (1698) attacked:

infoBite: Collier attacked Congreve, Vanbrugh, Dryden and Wycherley; Congreve replied, and the attack helped bring on sentimental comedy (Steele, Cibber).

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question: Why does Jean Baudrillard use Disneyland as his example of a sign?

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question:

(c) It plays with fixities and definites.
(d) It has a shaping and modifying power.

options.A: (a) and (b) for fancy; (c) and (d) for imagination
options.B: (a) and (c) for fancy; (b) and (d) for imagination
options.C: (b) and (c) for fancy; (a) and (d) for imagination
options.D: (c) and (d) for fancy; (a) and (b) for imagination

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question:
Julia Kristeva's concept of 'intertextuality' derives from:
(a) Saussure's signs
(b) Chomsky's deep structure
(c) Bakhtin's dialogism
(d) Derrida's différance
infoBite: Kristeva coined 'intertextuality' (1966, in 'Word, Dialogue and Novel') by combining Saussure's semiotics with Bakhtin's dialogism: every text is 'a mosaic of quotations'.

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question:
In Invisible Man, Ralph Ellison subverts myths of white purity through characters like:
(a) Norton
(b) Bledsoe
(c) Rinehart
(d) all of the above
infoBite: Mr Norton is the white trustee obsessed with his 'destiny'; Dr Bledsoe is the black college president who serves white power. Rinehart is the shape-shifting trickster of Harlem.

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question: Which of the following is NOT TRUE of Ralph Waldo Emerson?

options.A: He wrote essays on New England scenery, woodcraft and plantations.
options.B: He was an eloquent pulpit orator, a Unitarian in the tradition of William Ellery Channing.
options.C: In essays like "Nature" he stresses seeing familiar things in new ways.
options.D: His "The American Scholar" was delivered as an address before the Phi Beta Kappa Society at Cambridge in 1837.

infoBite: Essays on New England woods and woodcraft sound like Thoreau (Walden, The Maine Woods). Holmes called 'The American Scholar' (1837) 'our intellectual Declaration of Independence'.

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question: "The Exorcism" is the title of Act III of Edward Albee's Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf? What is its significance in the play?

options.A: The casting out of evil spirits
options.B: Deconstructing myths involving marriage, fertility and sons

infoBite: The three acts are 'Fun and Games', 'Walpurgisnacht' and 'The Exorcism', in which George 'kills' the imaginary son he and Martha invented.

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question: "Womanist is to feminist as purple is to lavender." This statement defines the womanist perspective advanced by:
works: In Search of Our Mothers' Gardens
infoBite: Alice Walker defines 'womanist' in the preface to In Search of Our Mothers' Gardens: Womanist Prose (1983).

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question: Characters in Golding's Lord of the Flies fit an allegorical pattern of virtues and vices. Identify the mismatched pair:
infoBite: Jack embodies savagery and the lust for power. The conch stands for order, and Piggy's glasses for science or intellect.

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question: A subaltern perspective is one where:

options.A: power structures define and determine your command of language and language of command in an uneven world
options.B: the politically dispossessed may be voiceless, written out of the historical record, and ignored because their activities do not count as 'cultural' or 'structured'
options.C: you do not know what your 'story' is or how to tell it, so you fall back on stereotyped situations to please your listeners
options.D: you begin to see how we live and have lived, how we have been led to imagine ourselves, and how our language has trapped and liberated us

infoBite: Gramsci's term was taken up by Ranajit Guha's Subaltern Studies group and by Spivak's 'Can the Subaltern Speak?' (1988).

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question:
Which statements about interlanguage are correct?
(a) 'Interlanguage' is a term we owe to M. A. K. Halliday.
(b) Interlanguage develops an autonomous and self-contained grammatical system.
(c) It is a distinct stage in a learner's progress in learning a second language.
(d) It owes nothing at all to either the learner's native language or the target language.
infoBite: Interlanguage is Larry Selinker's term (1972) for a learner's developing system, which draws on both the first language and the target language.
note: Answer from UGC's updated answer key for June 2012 (after grievances). CBSE's key gives C, but the term 'interlanguage' is Larry Selinker's, not Halliday's, so (a) is false. On the facts, only (c) is safely correct, and no option says that. Kept unverified for you to review.

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question: In a classic statement that inaugurated feminist thought in English we read: "A woman writing thinks back through her mothers." Where does this occur?

options.A: Virginia Woolf's A Room of One's Own
options.D: Mary Hiatt's The Way Women Write

infoBite: A Room of One's Own (1929) grew from Cambridge lectures; it imagines Shakespeare's sister Judith and says a woman needs 'money and a room of her own'.

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question:
Match the translators with their translations:
I. A. K. Ramanujan
II. Manmatha Nath Dutt
III. Mohini Chatterji
IV. Romesh Chunder Dutt

a. The Ramayana
b. The Bhagavad Gita
c. Speaking of Siva
d. The Mahabharata

Code: I II III IV
infoBite: Ramanujan's Speaking of Siva (1973) translates Kannada Virashaiva vachanas; R. C. Dutt condensed both epics into English verse (Ramayana 1899, Mahabharata 1898).

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question:
Assertion (A): In The Power and the Glory, Greene's whisky priest overcomes his fondness for drink and his human fears and moves towards martyrdom.
Reason (R): Transcendence in Greene's novels usually comes from love for humanity, but pride is also a key part of the priest's character.

options.C: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
options.D: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

infoBite: The Power and the Glory (1940) is set in 1930s Mexico during the persecution of the Church; the unnamed priest is hunted by a Marxist lieutenant and betrayed by the mestizo.
note: Answer from UGC's updated answer key for June 2012 (after grievances). Options are in a different order from usual: here C means 'both true, but R is not the correct explanation'.

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question:
Which statement about John Dryden is incorrect?
(a) John Milton and John Dryden were contemporaries.
(b) Dryden was a Royalist, while Milton fiercely opposed monarchy.
(c) Dryden wrote a play on the Mughal emperor Humayun.
(d) Dryden was appointed Poet Laureate of England in 1668.
infoBite: Dryden's Mughal play is Aureng-Zebe (1675), about Aurangzeb, not Humayun. He became Poet Laureate in 1668, the first official holder.

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question:
R. P. Blackmur, in "A Critic's Job of Work", likens criticism to walking: both are near-universal arts that call for constant balance, are hard to examine while in progress, and are rarely done well; most people prefer familiar paved walks and some form of rapid transport — a settled theory or dogma. Which of the following is correct?
(a) Blackmur compares criticism to walking because both are similar arts that demand close attention and care.
(b) Blackmur concedes that some people manage to be good at both criticism and walking.
(c) Critics favour tested approaches for the same reason walkers prefer paved paths and rapid transport.
(d) Blackmur does not actually supply equivalents of "some paved walks and some form of rapid transport" to support his comparison.
infoBite: Blackmur (1935) defines criticism as 'the formal discourse of an amateur' and is wary of all dogmatic methods. He was a key American New Critic (The Double Agent).

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question: Which mythological figure does William Blake use to represent a world dominated by cold, hypocritical materialists?
infoBite: Urizen ('your reason' / 'horizon') stands for reason, law and repression; his opposite is Orc (revolt), and Los is the imagination. Albion is the primeval man.

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question: Identify the correctly matched group:

options.A: Third Space – Wolfgang Iser; Hybridity – Edward Soja; Reception aesthetics – Ferdinand de Saussure; Langue – Homi Bhabha
options.B: Third Space – Ernst Bloch; Hybridity – Edward Said; Reception aesthetics – Eve K. Sedgwick; Langue – J. G. Frazer
options.C: Third Space – Edward Soja; Hybridity – Homi Bhabha; Reception aesthetics – Wolfgang Iser; Langue – Ferdinand de Saussure
options.D: Third Space – J. G. Frazer; Hybridity – Eve K. Sedgwick; Reception aesthetics – Edward Soja; Langue – Edward Said

infoBite: Soja's Thirdspace (1996) is geographical; Bhabha also uses 'Third Space' for hybridity in The Location of Culture (1994). Iser belongs to the Konstanz school of reception aesthetics.

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question: Which play is best described as (i) the first statement of Shaw's idea of the Life Force, (ii) a play about a woman's pursuit of her mate, and (iii) a play whose third act, 'Don Juan in Hell', is both unconventional and hilarious?
infoBite: Man and Superman (1903): Ann Whitefield pursues John Tanner, and the 'Don Juan in Hell' dream is often staged separately. Subtitle: 'A Comedy and a Philosophy'.

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question: Identify the untrue statement about the 'contact zone':

options.A: 'The contact zone' is a space where disparate cultures meet, clash and grapple with each other.
options.B: In postcolonial societies 'contact' suggests the historical moment when settler and indigenous cultures first met.
options.C: The idea of the contact zone was first proposed and defined in Mary Louise Pratt's Imperial Eyes: Travel Writing and Transculturation (1992).
options.D: The contact zone was largely instrumental in spearheading nationalist movements across the world.

infoBite: Pratt first used the term in her 1991 lecture 'Arts of the Contact Zone' and developed it in Imperial Eyes (1992), along with 'transculturation' and 'autoethnography'.

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
infoBite: Ceremony (1977) by Leslie Marmon Silko (Laguna Pueblo) is a landmark of the Native American Renaissance, alongside N. Scott Momaday's House Made of Dawn (1968).

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question: Which poem in Men and Women is addressed by Robert Browning to Elizabeth Barrett Browning?
infoBite: 'One Word More' (subtitled 'To E. B. B.') closes Men and Women (1855); the collection also includes 'Fra Lippo Lippi' and 'Andrea del Sarto'.

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question:

1. The Emperor Jones

3. After the Fall

infoBite: Williams – A Streetcar Named Desire (1947); O'Neill – The Emperor Jones (1920); Hansberry – A Raisin in the Sun (1959, title from Langston Hughes's 'Harlem'); Miller – After the Fall (1964).

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question:

1. Safdar Hashmi
2. Georg Kaiser

source: UGC NET June 2012 (24 Jun 2012, UGC) · Paper III
question:
Bertolt Brecht's Epic Theatre:
(a) turns the spectator into an observer
(b) wears down the spectator's capacity for action
(c) relies on argument
(d) presents man as a process

options.A: (a) and (d) are correct; (b) and (c) are incorrect
options.C: (b) and (d) are correct; (a) and (c) are incorrect

infoBite: From Brecht's table contrasting dramatic and epic theatre: epic theatre 'turns the spectator into an observer, but arouses his capacity for action'. It uses the alienation effect (Verfremdungseffekt).

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper II
question: Identify the work that does not belong to the literature of the eighteenth century:
infoBite: Bacon's The Advancement of Learning appeared in 1605. Gulliver's Travels (1726), The Spectator (1711–12) and Pope's Epistle to Dr Arbuthnot (1735) are all 18th-century.

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper II
question: Which of the following is a place that John Bunyan's Christian does NOT pass through?
infoBite: Mount Helicon is the Greek home of the Muses. Christian's route includes the Slough of Despond, the Interpreter's House, the Valley of Humiliation (Apollyon), Vanity Fair and Doubting Castle.

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper II
question: Queen Victoria reigned from:
infoBite: Victoria reigned from June 1837 to January 1901. The Reform Act of 1832 is often taken as the start of the Victorian literary period.

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper II
question: Which of the following statements about Lyrical Ballads is NOT true?

options.A: It carried only one ballad proper, Coleridge's The Rime of the Ancient Mariner.
options.B: It also carried pastoral and other poems.
options.C: It carried a Preface, which Wordsworth added in 1800.

works: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner
Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard
infoBite: Lyrical Ballads (1798) opened with 'The Rime of the Ancyent Marinere' and closed with 'Tintern Abbey'. The Preface came in 1800, and Wordsworth criticised Gray's diction in it (the 1802 version).

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper II
question: One of the following texts was published earlier than 1955. Identify it:
infoBite: Waiting for Godot was published in French in 1952 and first staged in 1953. The Inheritors, The Less Deceived and Empson's Collected Poems all appeared in 1955.

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper II
question: Which poets in 1930s England had left-leaning tendencies?

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper II
question: Name the theorist who divided poets into 'strong' and 'weak' and popularised the practice of 'misreading':
infoBite: Harold Bloom's The Anxiety of Influence (1973) and A Map of Misreading (1975) describe strong poets 'misprising' their precursors through six revisionary ratios such as clinamen and tessera.

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper II
question: In The Rape of the Lock, Pope repeatedly compares Belinda to:
infoBite: Belinda rivals the sun: 'Not with more glories, in th' ethereal plain, / The sun first rises o'er the purpled main' (Canto II). The poem is based on Lord Petre's cutting of Arabella Fermor's lock.

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper II
question: Which of the following awards is not given to Indian English writers?
infoBite: Until 2018 the Jnanpith went only to writers in the Eighth Schedule languages (Amitav Ghosh became the first English-language winner in 2018). The Whitbread (now Costa) goes to UK and Irish residents.
note: Answer from the updated answer key for December 2012 (after grievances), published on ugcnetonline.in. CBSE's updated key accepts both C and D. C is shown here.

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper II
question: Identify the correct statement:

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper II
question: W. M. Thackeray's Vanity Fair takes its title from:
infoBite: Vanity Fair: A Novel without a Hero (1847–48) takes its title from the town fair in Bunyan's allegory. Its heroine is Becky Sharp.

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper II
question: The Puritans closed all the theatres in England in:
infoBite: Parliament closed the theatres in September 1642 at the start of the Civil War; they reopened with the Restoration in 1660.

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper II
question: Which of the following was not a contemporary of Wordsworth and Coleridge?
infoBite: Swinburne (1837–1909) was a Victorian poet (Poems and Ballads, 1866). Southey, Scott and Hazlitt were all exact Romantic contemporaries.

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper II
question:

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper II
question:

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper II
question: Who is credited with making the first authoritative Dictionary of the English Language?
works: A Dictionary of the English Language
infoBite: Johnson's Dictionary (1755) took about nine years and defined some 42,000 words with literary quotations. His Plan of the dictionary was addressed to Lord Chesterfield.

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper II
question: In Dryden's An Essay of Dramatic Poesy (1668), who speaks first on behalf of the ancients?
infoBite: Crites (Sir Robert Howard) defends the ancients, Eugenius (Lord Buckhurst) the moderns, Lisideius (Sir Charles Sedley) the French, and Neander (Dryden) the English.

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper II
question: The term 'invective' refers to:

options.A: abusive writing or speech in which there is harsh denunciation of some person or thing
options.B: an insulting written attack upon a real person, in verse or prose, usually involving caricature and ridicule

options.D: the chanting or reciting of words deemed to have magical power

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper II
question: Which of the following novels depicts the plight of Bangladeshi immigrants in East London?
infoBite: Monica Ali's Brick Lane (2003) follows Nazneen, sent to London for an arranged marriage. White Teeth (Zadie Smith, 2000) is set in Willesden, and An Equal Music is Vikram Seth's.

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper II
question: The year 1939 was crucial for two important writers in England. Identify the correct statement:

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper II
question: The Enlightenment was characterised by:

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper II

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper II

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper II

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper II

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper II
question: Which of the following titles set a course for academic literary feminism?

options.D: A Dance to the Music of Time

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper II

infoBite: Tom Stoppard's Indian Ink (1995) moves between 1930 Jummapur, where the poet Flora Crewe sits for the painter Nirad Das, and 1980s England.

question: Shakespeare's sonnets:

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper II
question: Which of the following poems uses terza rima?

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper II

question: The term 'episteme' signifies:
infoBite: Greek epistēmē = knowledge. Foucault, in The Order of Things (1966), uses it for the underlying structure that decides what counts as knowledge in an age.

infoBite: Simonides called painting 'silent poetry' and poetry 'a speaking picture'; Sidney's Apology defines poetry as 'a speaking picture, with this end: to teach and delight'.
