infoBite: The theatres closed in 1642. The Commonwealth and Protectorate ran from Charles I's execution in 1649 to the Restoration in 1660. Davenant's 'operas' were staged quietly in the 1650s.
note: Answer from the updated answer key for December 2012 (after grievances), published on ugcnetonline.in. Remember the two dates: the closure order was in 1642, and the Commonwealth ran 1649–1660. CBSE's key goes with the Commonwealth years.

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper III
question: "To tell the truth, Shug act more manly than most men. I mean she upright, honest. Speak her mind and the devil take the hindmost…" What light does the quotation throw on Shug Avery?

options.B: She is upright and honest in asserting her lesbian identity.

infoBite: In The Color Purple (1982, Pulitzer 1983), the blues singer Shug Avery helps Celie find her voice. The novel is told mainly through Celie's letters to God and to Nettie.

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper III
question:
Which of these statements are correct?
1. A content word is not a function word.
2. A content word has less meaning than a function word.
3. A content word has no function.
4. A content word bears lexical meaning, whereas a function word has mainly grammatical meaning.
infoBite: Content words (nouns, main verbs, adjectives, adverbs) form open classes; function words (articles, prepositions, auxiliaries, conjunctions) form closed classes.

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper III
question: The year 1828 is a landmark in the history of American language and literature because:

options.A: Mark Twain's Adventures of Huckleberry Finn was published that year
options.B: The Southern Literary Messenger gained wide circulation from that year
options.C: Washington Irving was judged the nation's greatest writer that year
options.D: Noah Webster published An American Dictionary of the English Language that year

works: An American Dictionary of the English Language
infoBite: Webster's 1828 dictionary fixed American spellings such as color, center and theater. Huckleberry Finn came out in 1884–85.

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper III
question: What alternative title did Mary Shelley give to Frankenstein?
infoBite: Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus (1818) grew out of the 1816 ghost-story contest at the Villa Diodati with Byron, Percy Shelley and Polidori.

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper III
question: Which of the following statements about George Lamming's In the Castle of My Skin (1953) is not true?

options.A: On one level it is a coming-of-age story.
options.B: It is an elegiac account of a village's growth into awareness in the late colonial period.
options.D: It was George Lamming's first novel.

works: In the Castle of My Skin
infoBite: Lamming (Barbados) takes up The Tempest in his essays The Pleasures of Exile (1960), reading Caliban as the colonised, and in Water with Berries — not in this first novel.

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper III
question: We are likely to misunderstand an Emily Dickinson poem if we take her famous dashes to be:

options.C: suggestive of both forward and backward movements in sense

infoBite: Fewer than a dozen of Dickinson's nearly 1,800 poems were published in her lifetime. Thomas H. Johnson's 1955 edition restored her dashes and slant rhymes.

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper III
question:
Readers of Tayeb Salih's Season of Migration to the North will notice its parallels with:
I. Death in Venice
II. Othello
III. Bartleby, the Scrivener
IV. Heart of Darkness
works: Season of Migration to the North
infoBite: Salih's 1966 Arabic novel reverses Conrad's journey: Mustafa Sa'eed travels north to London. Mustafa insists 'I am no Othello. Othello was a lie.'

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper III
question: Which statement is NOT true of Benedict Anderson's Imagined Communities?

options.A: It is a prosaic response to the myth of El Dorado.
options.B: It is subtitled Reflections on the Origin and Spread of Nationalism.
options.C: In it Anderson argues that nations are not natural entities but narrative constructs.
options.D: For Anderson, modern nationalism grew from the convergence of capitalism, print technology and the fixity that print gave to vernacular languages.

infoBite: Imagined Communities (1983) coined 'print-capitalism'. Homi Bhabha's Nation and Narration (1990) builds on it.

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper III
question: "By swaggering could I never thrive, / For the rain it raineth every day." These lines from Feste's song in Twelfth Night are quoted in the novel:
infoBite: Each chapter of Middlemarch (1871–72) opens with an epigraph, many from Shakespeare. Feste's song ends Twelfth Night ('When that I was and a little tiny boy').

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper III
question: A mock-heroic poem:

options.A: mocks heroic pretensions in poets and critics
options.B: mocks heroism, an exaggerated virtue in all epics
options.C: uses a heroic style to deride airs and affectations
options.D: uses a mocking style to deride heroes and hero-worship

infoBite: Mock-heroic applies the grand epic style to a trivial subject (Pope's The Rape of the Lock). The opposite, treating a grand subject in a low style, is burlesque or travesty.

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper III
question: Which of the following is not true of Laurence Sterne's Tristram Shandy?

options.B: It opens and ends with the theme of birth (procreation).
options.C: It contains a trip to France.

infoBite: Tristram Shandy (1759–67) is famously digressive. It has a black page for Yorick, a marbled page and a blank page, and ends with a cock-and-bull story about Walter's bull.

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper III
question: In drama, an aside is addressed:

options.A: to the audience by an actor; the words are not meant to be heard by the other actors on stage
options.B: to other actors on stage; the words are not meant to be heard by the audience
options.C: by the playwright to the audience
options.D: by the protagonist to the antagonist

infoBite: An aside is brief and heard by the audience only. A soliloquy is a longer speech by a character alone on stage voicing their thoughts.

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper III
question:
Match the novels with their last lines:
i. The Mayor of Casterbridge
ii. Sons and Lovers
iii. The Great Gatsby
iv. The Mill on the Floss

1. "He walked towards the faintly humming, glowing town, quickly."
2. "In their death they were not divided."
3. "…happiness was but the occasional episode in a general drama of pain."
4. "So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past."

Code: i ii iii iv
infoBite: Hardy's last line is Elizabeth-Jane's reflection; Paul Morel turns towards the town; Nick Carraway's last line; Maggie and Tom drown together in the flood.

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper III
question: "There is nothing outside the text" is a statement by:
infoBite: 'Il n'y a pas de hors-texte' comes from Of Grammatology (1967), in Derrida's reading of Rousseau's Confessions.

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper III
question: Here is a list of women in Hardy's novels said to be abandoned by their lovers. Pick the odd one out:
infoBite: Bathsheba is pursued by Gabriel Oak, Boldwood and Troy, and finally marries Oak. Troy abandons Fanny Robin; Marty South (The Woodlanders) loses Giles Winterborne.

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper III
question: What is the following a definition of? "A loose sally of the mind; an irregular, indigested piece…"
works: A Dictionary of the English Language
infoBite: Johnson's Dictionary (1755) defines 'essay' as 'a loose sally of the mind; an irregular indigested piece; not a regular and orderly composition'.

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper III
question: Which of the following critics is not a New Critic?
infoBite: Lévi-Strauss was the French structural anthropologist (Structural Anthropology, 1958). Brooks and Warren wrote the New Critical textbook Understanding Poetry (1938).

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper III
question: Pick out the woman character who does not belong to Amitav Ghosh's novels:
infoBite: Ila is the narrator's cousin in The Shadow Lines (1988), and Piya (Piyali Roy) is the cetologist in The Hungry Tide (2004).
note: Answer from the updated answer key for December 2012 (after grievances), published on ugcnetonline.in. CBSE's key gives A (Ila), but Ila is a main character in Ghosh's The Shadow Lines, so the key looks wrong. Claude couldn't confirm which of the other three names is the outsider. Kept unverified for you to review.

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper III
question: Pick the odd man out among these members associated with the Subaltern Studies group:
infoBite: Sumit Sarkar was an early contributor who left the collective, criticising its turn to postmodernism ('The Decline of the Subaltern in Subaltern Studies', 1997).

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper III
question:
Statement (S): "Our birth is but a sleep and a forgetting."
Interpretation (I): The human soul never tires in the course of life; it never dies. Therefore human life is a long sleep, and ephemeral events are better forgotten.

options.A: (S) is a view and (I) is not correct.
options.B: (S) is a view and (I) is correct.
options.C: (S) is a poetic view; (I) does not suit it.
options.D: (S) is a poetic view and bears no relationship to (I).

infoBite: From stanza V of Wordsworth's 'Immortality Ode' (1807): the soul 'cometh from afar… trailing clouds of glory'.
note: Answer from the updated answer key for December 2012 (after grievances), published on ugcnetonline.in. CBSE's key gives B. In the ode, birth is a 'sleep' in which the soul forgets its heavenly origin, so many readers would choose C.

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper III
question: "You were silly like us; your gift survived it all: / The parish of rich women, physical decay, / Yourself." In Auden's view, what do these make of W. B. Yeats?
works: In Memory of W. B. Yeats
infoBite: From Part II of Auden's elegy (1939), which goes on: 'Mad Ireland hurt you into poetry… For poetry makes nothing happen'.

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper III
question: Which Dickens characters are "'umble" and "willin'"?
infoBite: Both are from David Copperfield (1850). Uriah Heep keeps calling himself 'umble', and the carrier Barkis sends Peggotty the message 'Barkis is willin''.

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper III
question:
'Fourth World literature' refers to:
I. the works of native peoples living in a land taken over by non-natives
II. the works of black people in the United States
III. the literature of the marginalised
IV. the works of non-heterosexuals

options.D: I, III and IV are correct

infoBite: The term comes from George Manuel's The Fourth World: An Indian Reality (1974). It covers indigenous writing such as Aboriginal Australian, First Nations and Maori literature.

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper III
question:
Assertion (A): In The Duchess of Malfi, Ferdinand sets a group of madmen on the Duchess, who dance and sing in a crazy manner.
Reason (R): His aim was to provide a strange entertainment that would drive the Duchess mad.
infoBite: Act IV: before her strangling, the Duchess says 'I am Duchess of Malfi still'. Ferdinand later says 'Cover her face; mine eyes dazzle: she died young'.

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper III
question: Why is Henry Louis Gates Jr.'s The Signifying Monkey a notable contribution to the study of African-American literature?

options.A: It focuses on largely neglected African-American novelists and poets.
options.B: It offers a theory of African-American criticism that draws on vernacular rhetorical practices of 'signifyin(g)'.
options.C: It offers a theory of African-American films and dramatic arts that signify the Black ethos.
options.D: It departs from critical theory of autobiographical narratives about Black lives and cultural traditions.

infoBite: The Signifying Monkey (1988) draws on the Yoruba trickster Esu-Elegbara and on 'signifyin(g)' — repetition with a difference — to explain how black texts answer one another.

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper III
question:
Identify the critic who:
I. wrote influential commentaries on Shelley, Blake and Yeats
II. published The Anxiety of Influence, A Map of Misreading, Poetry and Repression and The Western Canon
III. asserted that most literary criticism is only slightly disguised religion
IV. is arguably the most widely known and contrarian of his American peers in the academy
infoBite: The Western Canon (1994) puts Shakespeare at its centre. Bloom called critics of the canon the 'School of Resentment'.
note: Answer from the updated answer key for December 2012 (after grievances), published on ugcnetonline.in. Option B is printed as "Geoffrey Chaucer" on the source page; it is corrected here to Geoffrey Hartman, Bloom's Yale colleague.

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper III
question: According to the Italian Marxist theorist Antonio Gramsci:

options.B: hegemony involves a degree of consent on the part of the subject people
options.C: hegemony involves a degree of coercion on the part of a dominant political entity

infoBite: In the Prison Notebooks, hegemony is rule won through consent (civil society) backed by coercion (the state) — 'consent armoured by coercion'.
note: Answer from the updated answer key for December 2012 (after grievances), published on ugcnetonline.in. CBSE's key gives C, but the usual textbook answer is B (consent), since hegemony is what wins people's consent rather than ruling by force alone. Kept unverified for you to review.

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper III
question:
Match the groups with their names:
i. George Peele, Robert Greene, Thomas Lodge, Thomas Kyd
ii. William Congreve, William Wycherley, George Etherege, George Farquhar
iii. John Everett Millais, James Collinson, Ford Madox Brown, Dante Gabriel Rossetti
iv. Ernest Dowson, Lionel Johnson, W. B. Yeats

1. The Rhymers' Club / the Decadents of the 1890s
2. The Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood
3. The University Wits
4. The Restoration playwrights

Code: i ii iii iv
infoBite: The Rhymers' Club met at the Cheshire Cheese pub in Fleet Street from 1890. Kyd is usually grouped with the University Wits, though he did not attend university.

source: UGC NET December 2012 (30 Dec 2012, CBSE) · Paper III
question:
Combine the statements correctly. According to Homi Bhabha:
1. Mimicry is not mere copying or emulating of the coloniser's culture, behaviour and manners,
2. but it is further aimed at perfection and excess.
3. Mimicry is mere copying of the coloniser's culture, behaviour and manners,
4. but it is informed by both mockery and a certain menace.
infoBite: In 'Of Mimicry and Man' (1984), the colonial mimic is 'almost the same, but not quite' — a resemblance that also mocks and menaces colonial authority.

source: UGC NET June 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: The epithet "a comic epic in prose" is best applied to
infoBite: Fielding described his own kind of novel as a "comic epic poem in prose" in the Preface to Joseph Andrews (1742); Tom Jones (1749) is its fullest example.

source: UGC NET June 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: Muriel Spark has written a dystopian novel called

options.B: The Prime of Miss Jean Brodie

works: The Prime of Miss Jean Brodie
infoBite: All four are Spark novels: Robinson (1958), Memento Mori (1959), The Ballad of Peckham Rye (1960), The Prime of Miss Jean Brodie (1961). Spark was Scottish; Brodie is set in an Edinburgh girls' school.
note: Key B comes from a solved-paper site. None of the four is usually called dystopian, so the question itself is faulty; no official key was found.

source: UGC NET June 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: Samuel Butler's Erewhon is an example of
infoBite: Erewhon (1872) — roughly "nowhere" reversed — is a satirical utopia in which machines are banned and illness is punished as crime. Sequel: Erewhon Revisited (1901).

source: UGC NET June 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: The line "Monuments of unageing intellect" occurs in Yeats's
infoBite: "Sailing to Byzantium" opens The Tower (1928): "That is no country for old men." Its companion poem "Byzantium" came later, in The Winding Stair (1933).
note: The source prints "moments of unageing intellect"; the poem's actual word is "Monuments".

source: UGC NET June 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: In his 1817 review of Coleridge's Biographia Literaria, Francis Jeffrey grouped the following poets together as the 'Lake School of Poets':
infoBite: The Lake Poets — Wordsworth, Coleridge and Southey — were named after the Lake District where they lived. The hostile label came from Francis Jeffrey of the Edinburgh Review.

source: UGC NET June 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: Which of the following novels is not by Patrick White?
infoBite: Oscar and Lucinda (Booker 1988) is by Peter Carey. Patrick White won the Nobel Prize in 1973; The Tree of Man (1955), Voss (1957), The Vivisector (1970).

source: UGC NET June 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: The famous line "…where ignorant armies clash by night" is taken from a poem by
infoBite: It is the closing line of Arnold's "Dover Beach" (published 1867), a poem on the ebbing "Sea of Faith".

source: UGC NET June 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: Which among the following novels is not written by Margaret Atwood?
infoBite: The Stone Angel (1964) is Margaret Laurence's first Manawaka novel. Atwood: Surfacing (1972), The Handmaid's Tale (1985), The Blind Assassin (Booker 2000).

source: UGC NET June 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: The term 'theatre of cruelty' was coined by
infoBite: Artaud set out the Theatre of Cruelty in The Theatre and Its Double (1938). Boal created the Theatre of the Oppressed; Brustein wrote The Theatre of Revolt.

source: UGC NET June 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: The verse form of Byron's Childe Harold was influenced by
infoBite: Childe Harold's Pilgrimage (1812–18) is in Spenserian stanzas: nine lines rhyming ababbcbcc, the last an alexandrine. Keats's Eve of St Agnes uses the same stanza.

source: UGC NET June 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question:
Tennyson's Ulysses is
I. a poem expressing the need for going forward and braving the struggles of life
II. a dramatic monologue
III. a morbid poem
IV. a poem making extensive use of satire

Choose the correct combination according to the code:
infoBite: "Ulysses" (written 1833, published 1842) is a dramatic monologue ending "To strive, to seek, to find, and not to yield."

source: UGC NET June 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: Which post-war British poet was involved in a disastrous marriage with Sylvia Plath?
infoBite: Plath and Hughes married in 1956. Hughes became Poet Laureate in 1984; Birthday Letters (1998) is his verse account of the marriage.

source: UGC NET June 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question:
Chaucer's Parliament of Fowles is in part
I. a puzzle
II. a debate
III. a threnody
IV. a beast fable

Choose the correct combination according to the code:
infoBite: The Parliament of Fowls is a dream vision in rhyme royal, set on St Valentine's Day, where birds debate the choice of a mate — a debate poem and bird fable.
note: The source marks both A and D. Debate and beast (bird) fable are certain; whether 'a puzzle' was meant as correct is unclear. No official key was found.

source: UGC NET June 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: Who among the following wrote a book with the title The Age of Reason?
infoBite: Paine's The Age of Reason (1794–1807) argues for deism. His Rights of Man (1791) answered Burke's Reflections on the Revolution in France (1790).

source: UGC NET June 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: The Restoration comedy has been criticized mainly for its
works: A Short View of the Immorality and Profaneness of the English Stage
infoBite: Jeremy Collier's A Short View of the Immorality and Profaneness of the English Stage (1698) is the most famous attack on the comedy of manners.

source: UGC NET June 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: Ideology and Ideological State Apparatuses is an essay by
infoBite: Althusser's 1970 essay separates repressive state apparatuses (police, army) from ideological ones (school, church, family) and introduces 'interpellation'.

source: UGC NET June 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: Sexual possessiveness is a theme of Shakespeare's
infoBite: In A Midsummer Night's Dream, Oberon and Titania quarrel over the changeling boy, and Egeus claims the right to choose Hermia's husband.
note: Key D is from a solved-paper site; none of the other plays fits, but the wording is loose.

source: UGC NET June 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: The term 'Cultural Materialism' is associated with
infoBite: Williams used the term in Marxism and Literature (1977); Dollimore and Sinfield's Political Shakespeare (1985) made it a school. Greenblatt is linked to New Historicism.

source: UGC NET June 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: Which of the following author–book pairs is correctly matched?

options.B: William Golding – The Girls of Slender Means
options.D: Doris Lessing – The Grass is Singing

infoBite: The Grass is Singing (1950), set in Southern Rhodesia, was Lessing's first novel. Under the Net is Iris Murdoch's, The Girls of Slender Means is Spark's, Lucky Jim is Kingsley Amis's.
note: Option B is garbled in the source ("William – Girls of Golding Slender Means"); restored here.

source: UGC NET June 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: Who among the following is a Canadian critic?
infoBite: Frye's Anatomy of Criticism (1957) founded archetypal criticism. Richards and Leavis were British; Brooks was an American New Critic.

source: UGC NET June 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: Sethe is a character in
infoBite: In Toni Morrison's Beloved (1987; Pulitzer 1988), Sethe, an escaped slave, kills her daughter to save her from slavery. Lucy is by Jamaica Kincaid; Brewster Place by Gloria Naylor.

source: UGC NET June 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: Imagined Communities is a book by
infoBite: Benedict Anderson's Imagined Communities (1983) ties the rise of nationalism to print capitalism. Perry Anderson is his brother, a Marxist historian.

source: UGC NET June 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: Who among the following is a Cavalier poet?
infoBite: The Cavalier poets: Carew, Lovelace, Suckling and Herrick. Vaughan and Crashaw are Metaphysicals; Anne Finch wrote in the Augustan age.

source: UGC NET June 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: Which play of Wilde has the subtitle A Trivial Comedy for Serious People?
infoBite: The Importance of Being Earnest premiered in 1895, the year of Wilde's trials; its plot turns on Jack's invented brother 'Ernest'.

source: UGC NET June 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: Which of the following plays is not written by Wole Soyinka?
infoBite: 'Master Harold'… and the Boys (1982) is by South African Athol Fugard. Soyinka (Nobel 1986) wrote A Dance of the Forests for Nigeria's independence in 1960.

source: UGC NET June 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: Which of the following plays by William Wycherley is in part an adaptation of Molière's The Misanthrope?
infoBite: The Plain Dealer (1676): its hero Manly is modelled on Molière's Alceste. The Country Wife (1675) is Wycherley's best-known comedy.

source: UGC NET June 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: 'Inversion' is the change in the word order for creating rhetorical effect, e.g. "this book I like". Another term for inversion is
infoBite: Hyperbaton = departure from normal word order. Hypallage is the transferred epithet ("a sleepless night").

source: UGC NET June 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: The phrase 'the willing suspension of disbelief' occurs in
infoBite: Coleridge, Biographia Literaria (1817), Chapter XIV, on the supernatural poems of Lyrical Ballads: "that willing suspension of disbelief for the moment, which constitutes poetic faith."

source: UGC NET June 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: The religious movement Methodism in 18th-century England was founded by
infoBite: Methodism grew from the Oxford 'Holy Club' of John and Charles Wesley (1729); George Whitefield was its great field preacher.

source: UGC NET June 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: My First Acquaintance with Poets, an unforgettable account of meeting with literary heroes, is written by
infoBite: Hazlitt's essay (1823, in The Liberal) recalls hearing Coleridge preach at Shrewsbury in 1798 and visiting him and Wordsworth.

source: UGC NET June 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: The figure of the Warrior Virgin in Spenser's Faerie Queene is represented by the character
infoBite: Britomart, the female knight of Chastity, is the heroine of Book III and seeks her destined love Artegall. Gloriana is the Faerie Queene herself; Duessa stands for falsehood.

source: UGC NET June 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: The book Speech Acts is written by
infoBite: Searle's Speech Acts (1969) builds on J. L. Austin's How to Do Things with Words (1962), which introduced performatives and illocutionary acts.

source: UGC NET June 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: Which among the following is not a sonnet sequence?

options.D: D. G. Rossetti – The House of Life

infoBite: Omeros (1990) is Walcott's Caribbean epic in loose three-line stanzas, reworking Homer. Walcott won the Nobel in 1992.

source: UGC NET June 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: 'Incunabula' refers to

options.A: books censured by the Roman Emperor
options.C: books containing an account of myths and rituals
options.D: books wrongly attributed to an author

infoBite: Incunabula (Latin 'swaddling clothes, cradle') are books printed in Europe before 1501, in the infancy of printing.

source: UGC NET June 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: The most notable achievement in Jacobean prose was

options.B: King James' translation of the Bible

infoBite: The Authorized (King James) Version appeared in 1611, made by about 47 scholars. Burton's Anatomy of Melancholy came out in 1621.

source: UGC NET June 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: The Court of Chancery is a setting in Dickens'
infoBite: Bleak House (1852–53) centres on the endless Chancery suit Jarndyce and Jarndyce. Little Dorrit satirises the Circumlocution Office and the Marshalsea prison.

source: UGC NET June 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: Which Romantic poet coined the famous phrase 'spots of time'?
infoBite: "Spots of time" — memories with a renovating virtue — come in The Prelude (Book XI of the 1805 text, Book XII of 1850).

source: UGC NET June 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: The statement 'I think, therefore I am' is by
infoBite: 'Cogito, ergo sum' — first in French in Descartes' Discourse on Method (1637), later in Latin in the Principles of Philosophy (1644).

source: UGC NET June 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question:
Verse that has no set theme — no regular meter, rhyme or stanzaic pattern — is
I. open form
II. flexible form
III. free verse
IV. blank verse

Choose the correct combination according to the code:

options.A: I, II and III are correct
options.C: II, III and IV are correct

infoBite: Free verse (vers libre) is also called open form. Blank verse is different: unrhymed but in regular iambic pentameter.

source: UGC NET June 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: Which is the correct sequence of publication of Pinter's plays?

options.A: The Room, One for the Road, No Man's Land, The Homecoming
options.B: The Homecoming, No Man's Land, The Room, One for the Road
options.C: The Room, The Homecoming, No Man's Land, One for the Road
options.D: One for the Road, The Room, The Homecoming, No Man's Land

infoBite: The Room (1957, his first play) → The Homecoming (1965) → No Man's Land (1975) → One for the Road (1984). Pinter won the Nobel in 2005.

source: UGC NET June 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: Johnson's Dictionary of the English Language was published in the year
works: A Dictionary of the English Language
infoBite: Johnson's Dictionary (1755) took about nine years. Rasselas followed in 1759 and Lives of the Poets in 1779–81.

source: UGC NET June 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: The literary prize Booker of Bookers was awarded to
infoBite: Midnight's Children (Booker 1981) won the Booker of Bookers in 1993 and the Best of the Booker in 2008.

source: UGC NET June 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: In Keats' poetic career, the most productive year was
infoBite: 1819 brought the great Odes, The Eve of St Agnes, La Belle Dame sans Merci, Lamia and The Fall of Hyperion.

source: UGC NET June 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: Pope's The Rape of the Lock was published in 1712 in
infoBite: The 1712 version had two cantos; the 1714 version grew to five, adding the sylphs and gnomes. It was based on Lord Petre cutting Arabella Fermor's hair.

source: UGC NET June 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question:
Stephen Dedalus is a fictional character associated with
I. A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
II. Sons and Lovers
III. Ulysses
IV. Heart of Darkness

Choose the correct combination according to the code:
works: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
infoBite: Stephen Dedalus is Joyce's alter ego in A Portrait (1916) and Ulysses (1922), and in the early draft Stephen Hero. Sons and Lovers' hero is Paul Morel.

source: UGC NET June 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: In Moby Dick, Captain Ahab falls for his
infoBite: Ahab's monomaniac pride drives his hunt for the white whale. Moby-Dick (1851) is narrated by Ishmael; the ship is the Pequod.

source: UGC NET June 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: The first complete printed English Bible was produced by
infoBite: Coverdale's Bible (1535) was the first complete printed English Bible. Tyndale's printed New Testament came earlier (1526).

source: UGC NET June 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: Elizabeth Gaskell's novel Mary Barton is subtitled
infoBite: Mary Barton (1848) is a 'condition of England' novel. Sybil is subtitled The Two Nations (Disraeli); Middlemarch, A Study of Provincial Life (George Eliot).

source: UGC NET June 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: Some of the Jacobean playwrights were prolific. One of them claimed to have written 200 plays. The playwright is
infoBite: In the preface to The English Traveller (1633) Heywood claimed a hand in some 220 plays. His best-known is A Woman Killed with Kindness (1603).

source: UGC NET June 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: The concept of "star-equilibrium" in connection with man–woman relationship appears in
infoBite: In Women in Love (1920), Birkin wants a love with Ursula like two stars in balance — 'star-equilibrium'.

source: UGC NET December 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: Jeremy Collier's A Short View of the Immorality and Profaneness of the English Stage attacked, among others,
works: A Short View of the Immorality and Profaneness of the English Stage
infoBite: Collier's 1698 pamphlet attacked Congreve, Vanbrugh and Dryden; Congreve replied with Amendments of Mr. Collier's False and Imperfect Citations.

source: UGC NET December 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: The Crystal Palace, a key exhibit of the Great Exhibition, was designed by
infoBite: Paxton's glass-and-iron Crystal Palace housed the Great Exhibition of 1851 in Hyde Park. Edward Moxon was Tennyson's publisher.

source: UGC NET December 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: Influence of Indian philosophy is seen in the writings of
infoBite: The Waste Land (1922) ends with 'Datta, Dayadhvam, Damyata… Shantih' from the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad; 'The Dry Salvages' in Four Quartets draws on the Gita.

source: UGC NET December 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: In which of his voyages did Gulliver discover mountain-like beings?
infoBite: Gulliver's Travels (1726): I Lilliput (tiny people), II Brobdingnag (giants), III Laputa and others, IV the Houyhnhnms (rational horses) and Yahoos.

source: UGC NET December 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: Patrick White's Voss is a novel about
infoBite: Voss (1957) follows a German explorer crossing the Australian interior, loosely based on Ludwig Leichhardt; the desert landscape dominates the novel.

source: UGC NET December 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: Although Nobel Laureate Seamus Heaney writes in English, in voice and subject matter his poems are
infoBite: Heaney (Nobel 1995) was from County Derry, Northern Ireland. Death of a Naturalist (1966) includes 'Digging'; North (1975) has the bog poems.

source: UGC NET December 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: To whom is Mary Shelley's famous work Frankenstein dedicated?
infoBite: Frankenstein (1818) is dedicated to her father William Godwin, author of Political Justice. The story began in the 1816 ghost-story contest at Byron's Villa Diodati.

source: UGC NET December 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: Which among the following poems by Philip Larkin records his impressions while travelling to London by train?
infoBite: 'The Whitsun Weddings' (title poem of the 1964 collection) describes a train journey from Hull to London on which wedding couples board.

source: UGC NET December 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: The English satirist who used the sharp edge of praise to attack his victims was
infoBite: Dryden's satire works through mock praise: Mac Flecknoe (1682) crowns Shadwell king of Dullness, and Absalom and Achitophel admires Shaftesbury's talents while damning him.
note: No key was found for this paper. Dryden fits best (ironic praise in Mac Flecknoe and Absalom and Achitophel), but the question is loosely worded.

source: UGC NET December 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: One of the most famous moments of direct address to the reader — "Reader, I married him" — occurs in
infoBite: Jane Eyre (1847), Chapter 38, opens with this line. The novel was first published under the name Currer Bell.

source: UGC NET December 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: Langland's Piers Plowman is a satire on
infoBite: Piers Plowman is an alliterative dream vision and religious allegory that attacks corruption in the Church — friars, pardoners and greedy clergy.

source: UGC NET December 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: Which of the following thinker–concept pairs is correctly matched?
infoBite: Derrida launched deconstruction with Of Grammatology, Writing and Difference and Speech and Phenomena (all 1967). Archetypal criticism belongs to Northrop Frye; Eagleton is a Marxist.

source: UGC NET December 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: Sexual jealousy is a theme in Shakespeare's
infoBite: In Othello (c. 1603–04) Iago calls jealousy 'the green-eyed monster'; his handkerchief plot convinces Othello that Desdemona loves Cassio.

source: UGC NET December 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: The book titled The New Criticism, published in 1941, was written by
infoBite: Ransom's The New Criticism (1941) gave the movement its name. Brooks and Warren wrote Understanding Poetry (1938); Brooks, The Well Wrought Urn (1947).

source: UGC NET December 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: Which of the following is not a revenge tragedy?
infoBite: Kyd's The Spanish Tragedy (c. 1587) founded the English revenge tragedy; Webster's two plays follow it. Doctor Faustus is a tragedy of damnation, not revenge.

source: UGC NET December 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: Which of the following playwrights rejects the Aristotelian concept of the tragic play as imitation of reality?
infoBite: Brecht called his epic theatre 'non-Aristotelian': the alienation effect (Verfremdungseffekt) stops the audience from identifying and makes them think critically.

source: UGC NET December 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question:
The label 'Diasporic Writer' can be applied to
I. Meena Alexander
II. Arundhati Roy
III. Kiran Desai
IV. Shashi Deshpande

Choose the correct combination according to the code:

options.C: I, II and IV are correct

infoBite: Meena Alexander (memoir Fault Lines) lived and taught in New York; Kiran Desai won the Booker in 2006 for The Inheritance of Loss. Roy and Deshpande live and write in India.

source: UGC NET December 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question:
The letter 'A' in The Scarlet Letter stands for
I. Adultery
II. Able
III. Angel
IV. Appetite

Choose the correct combination according to the code:

options.C: I, II and IV are correct
options.D: I, II and III are correct

infoBite: Hester Prynne's 'A' means Adultery; as she serves the town people read it as 'Able', and an 'A' in the sky at Governor Winthrop's death is read as 'Angel'. Novel: 1850.

source: UGC NET December 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: A monosyllabic rhyme on the final stressed syllables of two lines of verse is called
infoBite: Masculine rhyme: one stressed final syllable (cat/hat). Feminine rhyme: stressed then unstressed (motion/ocean). Eye rhyme looks alike but sounds different (love/move).

source: UGC NET December 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: A fatwa was issued against Salman Rushdie following the publication of
infoBite: The Satanic Verses (1988) led to Ayatollah Khomeini's fatwa in February 1989. Grimus (1975) was Rushdie's first novel; Shame came in 1983.

source: UGC NET December 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: "There is nothing outside the text" is a key statement emanating from
infoBite: 'Il n'y a pas de hors-texte' is from Derrida's Of Grammatology (1967; English translation by Gayatri Spivak, 1976).

source: UGC NET December 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: The Augustan Age is so called because

options.A: King Augustus ruled over England during this period
options.B: English writers imitated the Roman writers during this period
options.C: the English King was born in the month of August
options.D: this was an age of sensibility

infoBite: Writers such as Pope, Swift and Addison modelled themselves on the poets of Emperor Augustus's Rome — Virgil, Horace and Ovid.

source: UGC NET December 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: One of the important texts of the Angry Young Men movement is

options.B: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man by James Joyce
options.D: The French Lieutenant's Woman by John Fowles

infoBite: Lucky Jim (1954) and John Osborne's Look Back in Anger (1956) are the key texts. Time's Arrow (1991) is by Kingsley's son Martin Amis.

source: UGC NET December 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: Whom does Alexander Pope satirise in the portrait of Sporus?
infoBite: In Epistle to Dr Arbuthnot (1735) Sporus is Lord Hervey ('this painted child of dirt'); Atticus is Addison.

source: UGC NET December 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: The hero of Marlowe's Tamburlaine was born a
infoBite: Tamburlaine (c. 1587) is a Scythian shepherd who conquers empires. Ben Jonson praised 'Marlowe's mighty line', the blank verse first shown here.

source: UGC NET December 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: In a letter to his brother George in September 1819, John Keats wrote of a fellow Romantic poet: "He describes what he sees — I describe what I imagine — Mine is the hardest task." The poet referred to is
infoBite: Keats was contrasting himself with Byron, the most famous poet of the day. The same journal-letter to George and Georgiana is full of comments on his own work of 1819.

source: UGC NET December 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: A sequence of repeated consonantal sounds in a stretch of language is
infoBite: Alliteration repeats consonant sounds, usually at word beginnings. Assonance repeats vowel sounds; consonance repeats consonants inside or at the end of words.
note: Option C is printed as 'Assent' in the source; read here as 'Assonance'.

source: UGC NET December 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: The Reformation was predominantly a movement in
infoBite: The Reformation began with Luther's Ninety-five Theses (1517). In England, Henry VIII's Act of Supremacy (1534) broke with Rome.

source: UGC NET December 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: The motto "only connect" is taken from

options.C: H. G. Wells' The History of Mr Polly

infoBite: 'Only connect…' is the epigraph of Howards End (1910), which links the cultured Schlegels with the business-minded Wilcoxes.

source: UGC NET December 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: English iambic pentameter was brought to its first maturity in
infoBite: Unrhymed iambic pentameter (blank verse) came in with Surrey's Aeneid translation and matured in Elizabethan drama — Marlowe's 'mighty line' and then Shakespeare.
note: No key was found for this paper. B fits the standard account (Marlowe's dramatic blank verse), but Chaucer's couplets could also be argued.

source: UGC NET December 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: Who among the following was not a member of the Bloomsbury Group?
infoBite: Bloomsbury included Virginia and Leonard Woolf, Vanessa and Clive Bell, Lytton Strachey (Eminent Victorians, 1918), Keynes, Roger Fry and Forster.

source: UGC NET December 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: The concept of the human mind as tabula rasa, or blank tablet, was propounded by
infoBite: Locke's Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1690) argues that all ideas come from experience. Sterne's Tristram Shandy plays on Locke's association of ideas.

source: UGC NET December 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: The terms 'resonance' and 'wonder' are associated with
infoBite: Greenblatt's essay 'Resonance and Wonder' (1990) is a New Historicist piece on how objects in museums are viewed. Terence Hawkes is linked to cultural materialism ('presentism').

source: UGC NET December 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: The metrical pattern used by Chaucer in the Prologue to The Canterbury Tales is
infoBite: The General Prologue is in rhyming couplets of ten-syllable (iambic pentameter) lines — the forerunner of the heroic couplet. Rhyme royal is used in Troilus and Criseyde.
note: The source says 'rhetorical pattern'; the question is about the metre.

source: UGC NET December 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: Charles Darwin's On the Origin of Species was published in the year
infoBite: On the Origin of Species appeared in 1859; The Descent of Man followed in 1871. Tennyson's 'Nature, red in tooth and claw' (In Memoriam, 1850) came before it.

source: UGC NET December 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: Who of the following is the author of Juno and the Paycock?
infoBite: Juno and the Paycock (Abbey Theatre, 1924) belongs to O'Casey's Dublin trilogy with The Shadow of a Gunman and The Plough and the Stars.

source: UGC NET December 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: The title of William Faulkner's The Sound and the Fury is taken from a play by
infoBite: From Macbeth's 'Tomorrow' speech (V.v): life 'is a tale / Told by an idiot, full of sound and fury, / Signifying nothing' — fitting Benjy's opening section (1929).

source: UGC NET December 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: "Silverman has never read Browning." This is an example of
infoBite: Naming the author for his works is metonymy (substituting an associated name). Zeugma: one word governing two others in different senses.

source: UGC NET December 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: The term 'Intentional Fallacy' was first used by
infoBite: Wimsatt and Beardsley's 'The Intentional Fallacy' (1946) was followed by 'The Affective Fallacy' (1949); both are in The Verbal Icon (1954).

source: UGC NET December 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question:
"Recessional: A Victorian Ode", Kipling's well-known poem,
I. laments the end of an era
II. marks a new commitment to scientific knowledge
III. expresses the sincerity of his religious devotion
IV. was occasioned by Queen Victoria's 1897 Jubilee celebration

Choose the correct combination according to the code:

options.A: I, II and III are correct
options.D: I, III and IV are correct

infoBite: 'Recessional' was written for Victoria's Diamond Jubilee (1897). Its refrain 'Lest we forget' warns that imperial pomp may become 'one with Nineveh and Tyre'.
note: No key was found. II is clearly wrong and IV clearly right; whether the examiner counted I and III as correct (D) or only III (B) can't be confirmed.

source: UGC NET December 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: Who among the following is not a Restoration playwright?
infoBite: Ben Jonson (died 1637) was an Elizabethan–Jacobean dramatist (Volpone, The Alchemist). Restoration drama began after theatres reopened in 1660.

source: UGC NET December 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: Which famous Romantic poem begins with the line 'Hail to thee, blithe Spirit! / Bird thou never wert'?
infoBite: Shelley's 'To a Skylark' was published with Prometheus Unbound in 1820. 'To the Cuckoo' and 'To the Daisy' are Wordsworth's; 'Ode to a Nightingale' is Keats's.

source: UGC NET December 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: Who among the following Victorian poets disliked his middle name?
infoBite: Hopkins (1844–89), a Jesuit priest, invented 'sprung rhythm'; his poems were published only in 1918, edited by Robert Bridges.
note: No official key. The solved-paper source and its commenters settled on Hopkins; the fact itself is hard to confirm.

source: UGC NET December 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: Aston is a character in Pinter's
infoBite: The Caretaker (1960) has three characters: brothers Aston and Mick and the tramp Davies. Stanley is in The Birthday Party; Ben and Gus in The Dumb Waiter.

source: UGC NET December 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question:
Byron's English Bards and Scotch Reviewers is about
I. a survey of English poetry
II. Evangelism in English poetry
III. the contemporary literary scene
IV. the early English travellers

Choose the correct combination according to the code:

options.B: II, III and IV are correct

infoBite: Byron's 1809 satire in heroic couplets answered the Edinburgh Review's attack on his Hours of Idleness and mocked contemporary poets such as Wordsworth, Southey and Scott.
note: No official key; I and III is the only combination that fits the poem.

source: UGC NET December 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: Which Eliotian character utters the question "Do I dare to eat a peach?"
works: The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock
infoBite: 'The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock' (1915) opens with an epigraph from Dante's Inferno. Stetson is hailed in The Waste Land; Sweeney appears in several poems.
note: The source prints the line as 'Do I eat a peach'.

source: UGC NET December 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: Which among the following works by Daniel Defoe landed him in prison and the pillory?

options.C: The Shortest Way with the Dissenters

works: The Shortest Way with the Dissenters
infoBite: The Shortest Way with the Dissenters (1702) ironically urged harsh measures against Dissenters. Defoe was pilloried in 1703 and wrote 'A Hymn to the Pillory'.

source: UGC NET December 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: The arrival of printing in fifteenth-century England was engineered by
infoBite: Caxton set up his press at Westminster in 1476; he printed The Canterbury Tales and Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur (1485).

source: UGC NET December 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: About which nineteenth-century English writer was it said that "He had succeeded as a writer not by conforming to the Spirit of the Age, but in opposition to it"?
infoBite: Hazlitt's The Spirit of the Age (1825) has portraits of contemporaries; in the essay on 'Elia' he says Lamb succeeded by going against the age.

source: UGC NET December 2010 (UGC) · Paper II
question: The Restoration comedy The Double Dealer was written by
infoBite: Congreve's The Double Dealer (1693) came after The Old Bachelor; his masterpiece is The Way of the World (1700).

question:
Passage: Special terms that need to be defined appear in all three types of studies: (a) qualitative, (b) quantitative, and (c) mixed methods. In qualitative studies, because of the inductive, evolving methodological design, inquirers may define few terms at the beginning; although they may advance tentative definitions. Instead, themes (or perspective or dimensions) may emerge through the data analysis. In the procedure section, authors define these terms as they surface during the process of research. This approach delays the definition of terms until they appear in the study, and it makes such definitions difficult to specify in advance in research proposals. For this reason, qualitative proposals often do not include separate sections for a definition of terms. Instead, writers pose tentative, qualitative definitions threaded throughout the study. In quantitative studies operating more within the deductive model of fixed and set research objectives, include extensive definitions early in the research proposal. Investigators may place them in separate sections and precisely define them. The researchers try to comprehensively define all relevant terms at the beginning of studies and to use accepted definitions found in the literature.

According to the passage, the qualitative researcher does not define all the concepts/terms because of:
infoBite: The passage is adapted from John W. Creswell's 'Research Design' (qualitative, quantitative and mixed methods).
note: Official NTA paper and answer key, from NETSET Corner's copy (geographercorner.com). Shift is inferred: posted with the 22 June Shift 1 Geography paper. Answer re-checked by Claude.

The materials utilized in the product are natural, industrially processed or may be recycled. The models of the product are ancient, revised traditional and fashionable. Handicraft is deeply frozen in society and contributes to the idea of preserving and perpetuating traditions. question:
Passage: As part of the great cultural renaissance generated during the post-independence period, there has occurred a most meaningful encounter with tradition in various fields of creative activity. The return to and discovery of tradition was inspired by a search for roots and a quest for identity. This was a part of the whole process of decolonization of our lifestyle, values, social institutions, creative forms and cultural modes.
The modern Indian theatre, product of a colonial theatrical culture, felt the need to search for roots most intensely to match its violent dislocation from the traditional course. Directors like B.V. Karanth, K.N. Panikkar and Ratan Thiyam have had a most meaningful encounter with tradition and, with their work, have reversed the colonial course of contemporary theatre and put it back on the track of the great Natyashastra tradition. It sounds paradoxical, but their theatre is both avant-garde in the context of conventional realistic theatre, and still belongs to the Natyashastra theatrical tradition.

The post-independence cultural renaissance in Indian theatre focused on:
infoBite: The passage says theatre felt the need to search for its roots after colonial dislocation.
note: Official Paper 1 of the English shift (copy posted on prepp.in) and NTA final answer key (Subject 030 English, 14-06-2023, First shift, Q-ID 30046). Answer re-checked by Claude.

source: UGC NET June 2023 · 14 June 2023 · Shift 2 · Paper 1
question:
Passage: Man is the only animal that laughs and weeps, for he is the only animal that is struck with the difference between what things are and what they ought to be. We weep at what exceeds our expectations in serious matters; we laugh at what disappoints our expectations in trifles. We shed tears from sympathy with real and necessary distress; as we burst into laughter from want of sympathy with that which is unreasonable and unnecessary. Tears are the natural and involuntary response of the mind overcome by some sudden and violent emotions. Laughter is the same sort of convulsive and involuntary movement, occasioned by mere surprise or contrast.
The serious is the stress which the mind lays upon the expectations of a given order of events and the weight attached to them. When this stress is increased beyond its usual intensity and strains the feelings by the violent opposition of good and bad, it becomes the tragic. The ludicrous is the unexpected relaxing of this stress below its usual intensity, by an abrupt transposition of ideas that takes the mind by surprise and startles it into a lively sense of pleasure.

According to the passage, which of the following is not true in the case of tears and laughter?

options.B: They are both the result of violent emotions
options.D: They are both reactions to experiences of the world

infoBite: Tears come from sudden, violent emotion; laughter from mere surprise or contrast.
note: Official Paper 1 of the English shift (copy posted on prepp.in) and NTA final answer key (Subject 030 English, 14-06-2023, Second shift, Q-ID 30546). Answer re-checked by Claude. Passage identified by Claude as the opening of William Hazlitt's 'On Wit and Humour' (Lectures on the English Comic Writers, 1819).
